title: Caring for the earth
hookLine: the earth is the great mother of the Japji's last salok

cards: Sikhs who recite the Japji in the morning end on its last salok, and it sounds less like the close of a hymn than a family introduction. Here is your teacher. Here is your father.
Here is your mother. And the names that follow aren't people. They're air, and water, and the ground under your feet.
After a long climb through the Japji's thought, it's a strange and lovely way to come down: back onto the earth, like a child into a lap.

teach.h: AIR THE GURU, WATER THE FATHER.
teach.b: First, the family. You met this salok's sound early on this path, when the Japji closed: pavan guru, pani pita, mata dharat mahat. In paraphrase: air is the Guru, water is the father, and the earth is the great mother.
A family, with roles. Air teaches, the way breath and sound carry the Word. Water gives life, the way a father is said to.
The earth holds and feeds. Second, the lap.
The salok goes on, in paraphrase: day and night are the two nurses, and the whole world plays in their lap. Light and dark take shifts, like two caregivers. Third, the reckoning.

Good and bad deeds are read out before the Lord, and each person's own actions bring them near or send them far. The child playing in the lap is also answerable for how it plays. Fourth, what family does.

teach.h: YOU DON'T STRIP YOUR MOTHER'S HOUSE.
teach.b: You don't strip your mother's house. You don't foul your father's water.
If the earth is the great mother, caring for it isn't a cause bolted onto faith; it's how you treat family.
Some Sikhs have taken the salok as the heart of environmental work, planting trees and cleaning rivers in its name. The Japji ends on the ground, among relatives, with the day's account still open.

how: Sikhs recite the Japji each morning, ending with the salok that calls air the Guru, water the father and the earth the great mother; some Sikh groups plant trees and clean rivers in its spirit.

games.q: what does “caring for the earth” mean?
o: treating the earth as the great mother, as family
a vow to live in the forest away from towns
a harvest festival held when the crops come in

games.q: the Japji's last salok: tap the pairs.

s: the Japji ends with a salok about air, water and earth
pavan guru, pani pita, mata dharat mahat.
in the salok, the earth is called the father
water is the father; the earth is the great mother.
the salok says the world plays with no account to give
good and bad deeds are read out before the Lord.

games.q: the salok has just called the earth your great mother. what does that ask of you?
o: care for her the way family cares for family.
keep away from the earth to keep it pure.
games.why: the child in the lap is answerable for how it plays: deeds are read out, near or far.

practice: Feel the air going in: the Guru, the salok says. Feel your weight on the floor or the ground beneath you: the great mother, holding you up without being asked.
Stay with that for a few breaths, and let one small piece of earth you could care for come to mind: a plant, a patch of ground, a tap left running.

wordCard.voice: Caring for the earth. The Japji's last salok calls air the Guru, water the father, and the earth the great mother; caring for her is how family treats family. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: mata dharat mahat, the earth, the great mother, from the Japji's last salok.

carryVoice: Your line: the great mother. Family looks after family, and the earth is family. Same time tomorrow.
